title: Classroom Assessment & Testing

points.sub: The standard to judge any test by
pts: A good test scores well on validity, reliability, practicality and washback — not just raw accuracy of marking.
Weakness in any one quality undermines the others, however well-designed the rest of the test is.
Use these four criteria to evaluate any test before adopting it, including ones in a coursebook.
points.who: Lyle Bachman & Adrian Palmer, "Language Testing in Practice"

items: Take a test you gave recently.
Answer four questions about it (see model language).
Score each quality: strong, adequate or weak.
Choose the weakest quality and make one change to the test.
Use the improved version next time and compare results.
Evaluate a textbook test or a previous board paper in the same way.
Work in pairs, evaluating each other’s tests.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Validity: Does it measure what I want to know about my learners?
Reliability: Would the same learner get a similar score on another day or with another marker?
Practicality: Can I give and mark it with the time and resources I have?
Washback: What kind of teaching and studying will this test encourage?

body: Purpose: a desk reference. Content: a square divided into four quadrants, each with an icon and a question: a target (‘Validity: right thing?’), a balance scale (‘Reliability: consistent?’), a clock (‘Practicality: feasible?’), a boomerang (‘Washback: effect on teaching?’). Style: clean, bold icons. Board version: four boxes.

items: Google Forms (free). Use the ‘Insights’ view after an auto-marked quiz to see which items most learners got wrong; items almost everyone gets wrong or right tell you little.

blocks.x: A paper checklist of the four questions attached to every test you write.

points.h: Validity: Testing What You Meant To
pts: A test is only useful if it measures the ability it claims to, not something adjacent to it.
A 'speaking test' that is actually a memorised-script recital test has a validity problem, however smoothly it runs.
Check validity before checking anything else — a reliable measurement of the wrong thing is still the wrong thing.

items: For each item on a test, write what it claims to test (for example, ‘listening for detail’).
Then write what a learner actually needs to do to answer it.
Mark any item where the two differ.
Rewrite those items.
Keep a list of common validity problems for future tests.
Ask learners what they had to do to answer a question.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A ‘listening’ test where learners must read long written questions: tests reading too.
A ‘speaking’ test where learners recite a memorized paragraph: tests memory, not speaking.
A ‘vocabulary’ test that asks for spelling from dictation: tests spelling and listening.

blocks.x: A fix: for the listening test, use short questions or pictures and read the questions aloud before playing the recording.

body: Purpose: to show validity. Content: two archery targets. On the first, arrows cluster tightly on a small target labelled ‘memorization’, while the real target, labelled ‘speaking’, is untouched. On the second, arrows cluster on ‘speaking’. Style: clean, simple. Board version: two circles.

items: None needed; this is a thinking task.

blocks.x: The test paper and a pencil.

pts: The same learner should get roughly the same score on different days or with different raters.
Inter-rater reliability is a particular challenge for speaking and writing, where scoring involves judgement.
Clear, shared marking criteria and rater training directly raise reliability.

items: Two teachers mark the same five essays independently using the same rubric.
Compare scores. Where they differ by more than one band, discuss why.
Agree on what each band means with examples (‘benchmark’ essays).
Revise the rubric wording where it caused disagreement.
Repeat each term with new samples.
For speaking, two teachers score the same recorded performances.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A three-band criterion that caused disagreement, and a revision:

lines: Before: Organization: good / fair / poor.
After: Organization: 3 = clear paragraphs, each with one main idea; 2 = paragraphs present but ideas mixed; 1 = no clear paragraphing.

blocks.x: Reliability improves when criteria describe what markers can see in the work.

body: Purpose: to show reliability. Content: two markers looking at the same essay. In the first panel, their score bubbles show ‘7’ and ‘4’; in the second panel, after agreeing criteria, both show ‘6’. Style: friendly, clear. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). Record both markers’ scores side by side and calculate differences.

points.sub: Comparing to whom, or to what
pts: Norm-referenced testing compares learners to each other, useful for ranking or selection.
Criterion-referenced testing compares against a fixed standard, like a CEFR can-do descriptor from Unit 2.
Choosing the wrong type for the purpose produces technically accurate but practically useless results.

items: Take a set of results and report them in two ways: by rank (norm-referenced) and against can-do statements (criterion-referenced).
Compare what each report tells the learner.
Decide which suits the purpose: selection, or guidance.
Use criterion-referenced reporting for classroom feedback.
Discuss with colleagues how school reports currently present results.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Norm-referenced: Anita came 18th out of 42.
Criterion-referenced: Anita can write a clear informal letter with correct past tenses. Next step: paragraphing.

blocks.x: The first tells Anita where she stands; the second tells her what to do next.

body: Purpose: to contrast the two kinds of referencing. Content: on the left, a queue of learners ordered by height, labelled ‘compared with others’. On the right, a single learner on a ladder of can-do rungs, labelled ‘compared with a standard’. Style: clean, inclusive. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free) to map scores to can-do levels.

blocks.x: A can-do checklist beside each learner’s marks.

pts: Washback is the effect a test has on what and how teachers teach in preparation for it.
A well-designed test produces positive washback, encouraging exactly the practice you'd want anyway.
A poorly designed test can distort teaching toward narrow test-taking tricks at the expense of real ability.

items: Before writing a unit test, ask: what do I want learners to practise before it?
Include at least one task that requires real communication (for example, writing a short message, a short speaking task).
Tell learners the test format in advance so they prepare for the right skills.
After the test, note how learners prepared.
Adjust future tests to encourage better preparation.
Share the test criteria with learners before they study.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Test A: 30 multiple-choice grammar items. Likely preparation: memorizing rules and practising multiple choice.
Test B: 10 grammar items + a short email + a two-minute speaking task. Likely preparation: writing and speaking practice.

blocks.x: Alderson and Wall (1993) cautioned that washback is complex and not always predictable, but the direction of a test’s influence is usually clear enough to design for.

body: Purpose: to illustrate washback. Content: a test paper throwing a boomerang backwards in time towards a classroom, where it lands and changes what is on the board. Style: playful, clear. Board version: an arrow looping back.

items: None needed.

blocks.x: The test outline shared with learners on the board.

pts: A test should mirror the real-world skill it claims to assess, not just a written proxy for it.
A multiple-choice test of listening comprehension tests something narrower than genuine listening ability in use.
Where practicality allows, prefer task formats that resemble authentic skill use over simplified proxies.

v: Four short task types (see model language)

items: Replace one traditional test item per skill with a task that resembles real use.
Listening: a short announcement with a practical question.
Reading: a real notice or message with a decision to make.
Writing: a short message to a real reader.
Speaking: a short conversation or picture description.
Mark with a simple rubric.
In large classes, test speaking by rotating a small group each lesson.
Support: pictures accompany questions.
Stretch: an extra part requiring an opinion.

lines: Listening: Listen to the school announcement. What time does the sports day start, and what should you bring?
Reading: Read the bus timetable. Which bus should you take to arrive before 9?
Writing: Write a short message to your friend saying you can’t come to her birthday and why.
Speaking: Describe your favourite place in your town to the examiner for one minute.

body: Figure 21.6 Test tasks that look like life

Purpose: to show authenticity. Content: four small panels, each pairing a real-life situation with a test task: a railway platform (listening), a bus stop timetable (reading), a phone message (writing), two people talking (speaking). Style: consistent, clean illustrations. Board version: not applicable.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in) for recording speaking tasks for later scoring.

blocks.x: Teacher reads listening texts aloud; real notices photocopied or copied onto the board.

pts: Portfolios, can-do checklists and continuous assessment complement or can replace a single high-stakes test.
These formats capture development over time, which a one-off test by definition cannot.
They also reduce the disproportionate stress a single test event places on performance.

blocks.x: A term without a single big test

v: Portfolio folder; can-do checklists; observation notes

items: Plan assessment for one term as a combination: portfolio of three pieces of work, two can-do self-assessments, observation notes, and one short test.
Explain the plan to learners and parents.
Collect evidence steadily across the term.
At the end, combine evidence into a short report.
Compare with a previous term’s single-test results: which gave a fuller picture?
Use this approach for one skill only (writing) at first.
Support: fewer portfolio pieces with more support.
Stretch: learners choose and justify their best pieces.

lines: Portfolio: a letter (draft and final), a story, a poster.
Self-assessment: can-do ladder in week 3 and week 12.
Observation: notes from pair tasks.
Short test: a 20-minute reading and listening check.

body: Purpose: to show assessment as a collection. Content: a folder open on a desk, with several items spilling out: a letter with drafts, a poster, a can-do checklist, a sticky note with observations, and a small test paper. Caption: ‘a fuller picture’. Style: warm, realistic. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Drive folders (free) for digital portfolios where devices are available.

blocks.x: A paper folder per learner kept in class.

body: The NEP 2020 proposes a holistic, 360-degree progress card that includes self-assessment, peer assessment and teacher assessment, and reports on learners’ progress across a range of abilities, not only marks in examinations (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The alternatives in this point are practical steps in that direction.

pts: A test score is a snapshot of performance on that day, not a permanent verdict on a learner's ability.
Communicate results in a way that supports the learner's next steps, not just ranks them against peers.
This closes the loop back to Unit 2 — assessment results feed forward into an updated learner profile.

items: For each learner, write three short lines: one strength, one area to work on, one specific next step.
Avoid comparing the learner with others.
Share the report with the learner, and invite a response.
Revisit the next step at the start of the following term.
Learners write their own three lines first, then compare with the teacher’s.
Not applicable (teacher activity).

lines: Strength: You write clear, friendly letters and use past tenses correctly.
To work on: joining ideas with linking words.
Next step: in your next three pieces, use because, however and so at least once each.

blocks.x: A score is a snapshot of one day; a next step is a direction for the next term.

body: Purpose: to show next-step reporting. Content: a report card with three rows (‘strength’, ‘to work on’, ‘next step’) and an arrow from the ‘next step’ row pointing off the page towards a signpost labelled ‘next term’. Style: clean, encouraging. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free) report template.

blocks.x: A three-line paper report stapled into the learner’s notebook.

body: For one class, add a single ‘next step’ sentence to every learner’s marks this term. At the start of next term, ask learners whether they remember their next step. The answer will tell you whether the report was read as a direction or just as a grade.

dek: Unit 21 of 100: what makes a test worth trusting — validity, reliability, practicality and washback — and where alternatives to formal testing fit alongside it.

aims.x: This unit introduces the qualities that make a language test trustworthy and shows how to apply them to classroom tests. It also looks at alternatives to formal testing and at reporting results in ways that help learners move forward.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: evaluate any test for validity, reliability, practicality and washback;
check whether a test measures what it claims to measure;
improve the consistency of scoring for speaking and writing;
choose between norm-referenced and criterion-referenced reporting;
design tests that encourage good teaching;
test the four skills in ways that resemble real use;
use portfolios, checklists and continuous assessment;
report results as a guide to next steps.

why: Why this matters. Unit 8 covered day-to-day feedback. Formal assessment carries higher stakes and needs its own standards — a poorly designed test can undo good teaching.

background.x: Tests are everywhere in education, and English is no exception. Learners face unit tests, term examinations, board examinations, entrance tests and, for some, international proficiency tests. Teachers write many of these themselves, often at short notice and with little training in test design. Yet the results can affect learners’ confidence, their opportunities and the way teachers teach.

Language testing specialists have developed a clear set of criteria for judging tests. Lyle Bachman and Adrian Palmer (1996) describe the ‘usefulness’ of a test in terms of several qualities, including reliability, construct validity, authenticity, interactiveness, impact and practicality. Arthur Hughes (2003) presents similar ideas for classroom teachers in accessible form. This unit uses four core qualities, validity, reliability, practicality and washback, because they are the ones a teacher can check quickly for any test.

Classroom assessment has also broadened. Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam (1998) showed the power of formative assessment, used to guide teaching rather than only to grade learners. The National Education Policy 2020 recommends a move towards regular, formative, competency-based assessment and a holistic progress card that reports on learners’ development across many areas, not only marks (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The principles in this unit support that shift. Unit 57 returns to washback and test design in depth, and Unit 73 to the ethics of high-stakes testing.

items: Test audit. Teachers apply the four-quality checklist to three tests and record improvements.
Marker agreement. Track the difference between two markers’ scores before and after moderation.
Authentic task use. Count how many test tasks resemble real use; aim to increase the number each term.
Report quality. Check that learner reports contain a specific next step.
What does your most recent test reward: knowledge, memory, or ability to use English?
How consistent is your scoring of speaking and writing? How do you know?
How do your learners prepare for your tests? Is that the preparation you want?
What would learners and parents need in order to value evidence other than test scores?
What does a mark tell a learner about what to do next?

terms.def: Assessment that asks learners to perform tasks resembling real-world language use, such as writing a letter to a newspaper or conducting an interview, rather than answering isolated test items.
An agreed standard or reference point for judging performance, often illustrated by examples of work at each level, so that different teachers interpret a scale in the same way.
The ability or quality a test aims to measure, such as reading comprehension or speaking fluency; a clear definition of the construct is the basis for valid assessment.

Describes assessment that judges performance against fixed criteria or standards, rather than against the performance of other learners; contrast norm-referenced assessment, which ranks learners against one another.
A report card recommended by NEP 2020 that describes a learner’s development across many areas, including self- and peer assessment, rather than reporting marks alone.
The degree to which different markers give the same score to the same performance. It is improved by clear rubrics, benchmark samples and standardization meetings.
Feedback that tells a learner specifically what to do next to improve, such as ‘Add a reason to each opinion’, rather than simply giving a grade or general praise.
Describes assessment that reports a learner’s performance in relation to other test takers, for example by rank or percentile, rather than against fixed criteria.
A purposeful collection of a learner’s work over time, often with reflections, which shows progress and supports assessment for learning.

1. In assessment, whether a test is feasible given time, cost and resources. 2. In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teachers should theorize from their practice and practise what they theorize.

The consistency of a test’s results: whether the same learner would get a similar score on another day, with another marker or on another version of the test. Clear marking criteria and marker training improve reliability.

A scoring guide that sets out the criteria for assessing a piece of work and describes performance at each level. Shared in advance, a rubric makes expectations clear and supports self-assessment and peer assessment.
The extent to which a test measures what it claims to measure and supports the decisions made with its scores. A speaking test that only checks written grammar has low validity.

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
